content: Most of this pack is a thousand years old;
these twenty are not. Modern German handed
them across in the last two centuries, and
English kept them whole because nothing of
its own said the same thing.
kindergarten  Kinder + Garten
wanderlust    wandern + Lust
poltergeist   poltern + Geist
rucksack      Rücken + Sack
The parts are cousins of English parts:
garden, lust, ghost, sack. Flak folds a whole
gun, Fliegerabwehrkanone, into four letters.
When a word is exactly right, nobody
translates it.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: borrowed whole.
A calque is a loan translation: the German
compound taken apart and rebuilt from English
pieces, so that nothing foreign shows on the
surface. Loanword itself is one, made from
Lehnwort, loan and word.
loanword     Lehnwort
superman     Übermensch
masterpiece  Meisterstück
earworm      Ohrwurm
Brainwash is the same trick on a Chinese
phrase. The rest came across whole: the
miners' cobalt, quartz and feldspar, and
schadenfreude, joy at another's harm, which
no English parts could be found to carry.
THE NEXT 16 CARDS: calques and loans.
Thirty words that Old English left standing
on their own. Some kept the old sense at the
edge of speech, in verse, in Scots, in set
phrases: weird was wyrd, what befalls; hale
is whole and sound; woe was a cry of grief.
weird     Old English wyrd, fate
hale      Old English hal, whole
bane      Old English bana, a slayer
smite     Old English smitan, to strike
The others are fossils of the old grammar:
oxen and children keep the -en plural; shone
and shorn change the vowel where -ed would
do; wrought is the past of work; dreamt,
leapt and spilt keep the -t past beside -ed.
THE NEXT 30 CARDS: survivals and fossils.
-FUL is Old English full, the adjective hung
on the end of a noun: hopeful is full of hope.
-LESS is Old English leas, free of, without:
hopeless is without hope. Friendly opens the
cluster with the third ending, -ly, Old
English lic, a body: in the shape of a friend.
hopeful     hope + ful
hopeless    hope + less
fearless    fear + less
mirthful    mirth + ful
Some keep a noun that has since gone: ruth,
pity, survives only in ruthless; list, desire,
only in listless. Bountiful and plentiful
hang the English ending on a French noun.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: -ful and -less.
-LING is Old English -ling, an ending that
names a person or creature by what marks it:
a weakling is one who is weak, a foundling
one who was found. On animals it means the
young: duckling, gosling, nestling. It can
also look down: an underling, a hireling.
weakling    weak + ling
darling     dear + ling
duckling    duck + ling
sibling     sib + ling
Sib is the old word for kin, and darling is
dear and ling with the vowel worn down.
Fledgling stands beside novice, its Norman
twin, the French for one newly come.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: words in -ling.
Five endings that name a direction or a
trade. -WARD is Old English -weard, turned
toward: homeward, skyward. -WRIGHT is wyrhta,
a worker, kin to wrought. -SMITH is smith,
the worker in metal. -STER, Old English
-estre, was once the woman's ending, and
-MONGER, mangere, a dealer, is Latin mango.
playwright   play + wright
blacksmith   black + smith
spinster     spin + ster
fishmonger   fish + monger
Spinster was a trade before it was a state,
brewster the woman who brewed. Blacksmith
stands beside farrier, the French ferrier.
THE NEXT 24 CARDS: the craft suffixes.
Three endings that turn a person or a thing
into a state or a realm. -DOM is Old English
dom, judgment, the word doom: an earl's dom
is where his judgment runs. -HOOD is had, a
rank or condition. -SHIP is scipe, from the
verb to shape: the shape a thing is in.
wisdom       wise + dom
earldom      earl + dom
childhood    child + hood
worship      worth + ship
Worship is worthiness before it is a rite.
Earldom stands beside county, the land of a
Norman count; dukedom beside duchy, the same
land in the French.
THE NEXT 16 CARDS: -dom, -hood and -ship.
A kenning is the Old English poet's name for
a thing he will not call by its name: two
plain nouns set together into a small riddle.
The sea is the whale-road; the body is the
bone-house; blood is battle-sweat; the lord
who pays his men is the ring-giver.
whale-road    the sea
bone-house    the body
word-hoard    all a speaker commands
sky-candle    the sun
The habit never died. Bookworm, war-hawk,
swan-song and hell-bent are kennings made in
modern English by the same rule: two things
side by side, and the reader sees the third.
THE NEXT 18 CARDS: kennings.
Twenty words that hide their parts. In tier 2
the seams had healed; here they have vanished,
and often one half is a word that died: thirl,
a hole, lives only in nostril; dige, a
kneader, only in lady; were, a man, only in
werewolf.
daisy       daeges eage, the day's eye
lady        hlaf + dige, loaf kneader
nostril     nose + thirl, nose hole
sheriff     shire + reeve
Some took a Latin letter: island got its s
from insula, though ig-land is English through
and through. Gospel is good spell, good news,
the English for the Greek euangelion.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: hidden etymologies.
In 1822 Jacob Grimm, the collector of the
tales, set the Latin and Germanic words for
the same things side by side and saw the
consonants had shifted, not at random but
by rule. Where Latin keeps p, t and k,
Germanic has f, th and h.
father    Latin pater    f for p
thou      Latin tu       th for t
horn      Latin cornu    h for k
hound     Latin canis    h for k
The twin on each card keeps the Latin
side: paternal, canine, dental. Once
seen, the shift cannot be unseen: every pair
of Romance and Germanic cousins rides it.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: Grimm's Law cognates.
The cousins across the water share a root
and have gone their own ways. The shape is
the same; the sense is not, and a reader of
German meets the trap from both sides.
gift     German Gift      poison
fast     German fast      almost
bald     German bald      soon
mist     German Mist      dung
Toll is splendid there and a tax here; a
Stall is a stable; a Fall is a case at law;
a Handy is a mobile phone, coined from
English and sent back. Boot and Boot are no
kin at all. A few kept faith: stink and
bitter mean what they meant on both shores.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: cognates and false friends.
Two plain words, and the sum is a picture,
not a description. A brainstorm is a storm
inside the brain; a foxglove is a glove for a
fox; a toadstool is a stool for a toad, from
the belief that toads sat on the deadly kinds.
brainstorm   brain + storm
nightmare    night + mare
foxglove     fox + glove
eyesore      eye + sore
Some pictures have lost a piece. The mare in
nightmare is a crushing spirit, not a horse;
the cob in cobweb is coppe, a spider; warlock
is waer and loga, an oath breaker. The
picture outlived the word that drew it.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: metaphor compounds.
A thousand words, and every one of them
the plain word underneath: the English that
was here before the French and the Latin
were laid over it, and is still the floor.
You will hear it from now on. When somebody
says begin instead of commence, or buy
instead of purchase, you will know they
reached for the oldest layer. The seams
reopen once you can see them: break and
fast, hand and book, give and up.
Across the water the cousins keep the other
half: Sonnenlicht for sunlight, Handbuch for
handbook, shown here and never spoken. The
same words, worn another way.
The oldest layer is yours.
